subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: What is the equals() method in Java used for, and how does it differ from the == operator when comparing two objects?
reference_answer: When applied to two reference variables, == only checks whether they point to the SAME memory location (the same object). equals() is designed to compare LOGICAL/content equality (for example, two Student objects with the same student ID are considered equal even though they are different objects in memory). The default implementation of equals() in Object actually still uses ==, so any class that needs content-based comparison must override equals().
key_points: == compares identity (same reference), equals() compares logical/content equality
Object's default equals() behaves like ==; override it for content-based comparison

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: What value does hashCode() return and which data structures mainly use it?
reference_answer: hashCode() returns an integer (int) representing the object, used as a 'hash code' to determine the location (bucket) where the object is stored in hash-based structures such as HashMap, HashSet and Hashtable. Thanks to hashCode, these structures can quickly narrow the search before calling equals() for an exact comparison.
key_points: hashCode() returns an integer used as the object's hash code
HashMap and HashSet use it to pick a bucket before comparing with equals()

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: Why should you override toString() in your own classes?
reference_answer: By default, Object.toString() returns a string like ClassName@hexCode (e.g., Student@1b6d3586), which carries almost no useful information. Overriding toString() gives a readable representation of the object's state, which is very helpful for logging, debugging, IDE inspection and error messages. However, sensitive data (passwords, tokens) should not be included in toString().
key_points: Default toString() only returns the class name and a hex hash code
Overriding toString() helps logging/debugging, but avoid exposing sensitive data

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: Object as the root of all classes
question: What role does the Object class play in Java's class hierarchy?
reference_answer: Object is the root of Java's entire inheritance tree: any class that does not explicitly extend another class implicitly extends Object. As a result, every object has common methods such as equals(), hashCode(), toString() and getClass(), and a variable of type Object can refer to any object.
key_points: Every Java class implicitly extends Object if it extends no other class
Object provides common methods such as equals, hashCode, toString, getClass

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: What is the Comparable<T> interface in Java used for? Which method must be implemented?
reference_answer: Comparable<T> defines the 'natural ordering' of a class's objects. The implementing class must write int compareTo(T other), returning a negative number if the current object is smaller than other, 0 if equal, and a positive number if larger. Objects can then be sorted with Collections.sort() or used in TreeSet/TreeMap without supplying an extra comparator.
key_points: Comparable defines an object's natural ordering via compareTo()
compareTo returns negative/0/positive for less than/equal/greater than

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: How does Comparator<T> differ from Comparable<T>?
reference_answer: Comparable is implemented INSIDE the class being compared and allows only one natural ordering. Comparator is a SEPARATE comparison object outside the class (implementing int compare(T a, T b)), allowing many different orderings (by name, by score, by date of birth...) without modifying the class's source code, even for third-party library classes.
key_points: Comparable lives inside the class and gives a single natural ordering
Comparator is external and allows many sort criteria without changing the original class

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: What is an enum in Java, and why should you use an enum instead of int constants (e.g., STATUS_NEW = 0, STATUS_CANCELLED = 1)?
reference_answer: An enum is a special type that defines a finite set of named constant values (e.g., enum Status { NEW, PROCESSING, CANCELLED }). Compared to int constants, enums are type-safe: the compiler prevents passing an arbitrary invalid integer, code is more readable, enums can be used in switch, and each enum value can carry its own fields and methods.
key_points: An enum is a finite set of named constants and a type of its own
Type-safe, readable, can have fields/methods — better than int constants

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: What is a record in Java (since version 16), and what kind of data is it suited for?
reference_answer: A record is a concise class declaration for objects that only carry immutable data (data carriers), e.g., record Point(int x, int y) {}. The compiler automatically generates the constructor, accessor methods (x(), y()), equals(), hashCode() and toString(). A record's fields are final, so records are well suited for Value Objects, DTOs and returning multiple values.
key_points: A record is an immutable data class with auto-generated constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode, toString
Suited for pure-data Value Objects/DTOs

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: What is special about a non-static inner class in Java compared to a regular class?
reference_answer: An inner class (non-static nested class) is declared inside another class, and each of its objects is always tied to a specific object of the enclosing (outer) class. Therefore it can directly access all members of the enclosing object, including private ones. To create an inner class object you need an existing outer object (outer.new Inner()).
key_points: An inner class is bound to a specific instance of the enclosing class
It can access even private members of the enclosing class

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: What is the core difference between a static nested class and a (non-static) inner class?
reference_answer: A static nested class does not hold a reference to any object of the enclosing class; it behaves like an independent class that is merely placed in the outer class's namespace for logical grouping. Hence you can create it without an outer object (new Outer.Nested()), and it can only directly access the static members of the outer class.
key_points: A static nested class neither needs nor holds a reference to an outer object
It only directly accesses the outer class's static members; used to group related classes

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: What is an anonymous class and when is it typically used?
reference_answer: An anonymous class is a class without a name, declared and instantiated in place, usually to quickly implement an interface or extend a class for one-off use, e.g., new Comparator<Student>() { public int compare(...) {...} }. It is commonly used for callbacks, UI event handling, or short implementations that do not justify a separate class.
key_points: An anonymous class is declared and instantiated in place, without a name
Used for one-off implementations such as callbacks and listeners

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: What is a lambda expression in Java and which construct can it replace?
reference_answer: A lambda is a concise syntax for an anonymous function, of the form (parameters) -> expression or block, e.g., (a, b) -> a.getScore() - b.getScore(). A lambda can only be used where a functional interface (an interface with exactly one abstract method) is expected, and it typically replaces an anonymous class implementing that interface, making code shorter and more readable.
key_points: A lambda is an anonymous function with syntax (params) -> body
Used instead of anonymous classes when the target type is a functional interface

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: What is a functional interface? What does the @FunctionalInterface annotation do?
reference_answer: A functional interface is an interface with EXACTLY ONE abstract method (it may have additional default/static methods), e.g., Runnable, Comparator, Function<T,R>, Predicate<T>. It is the target type for lambdas and method references. The @FunctionalInterface annotation asks the compiler to check and report an error if the interface has more than one abstract method, protecting the design intent.
key_points: A functional interface has exactly one abstract method
@FunctionalInterface makes the compiler enforce this constraint

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: What are packages in Java used for in organizing object-oriented code?
reference_answer: A package groups related classes/interfaces into a single namespace (e.g., com.company.sales.order). It helps avoid class-name conflicts between libraries, organizes source code by feature/module, and works with the default (package-private) access modifier to restrict access to within the same package.
key_points: A package groups related classes into a namespace
Avoids name conflicts and supports package-level access control

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: The final keyword with reference variables
question: Does declaring final List<String> list = new ArrayList<>(); make the list immutable (no adding/removing elements)? Explain.
reference_answer: No. final on a reference variable only prevents REASSIGNING the variable to another object (list = new ArrayList<>() would be a compile error). The object the variable points to can still change state normally, so list.add(...) and list.remove(...) are still valid. For an immutable list you must use List.of(...) or Collections.unmodifiableList(...).
key_points: final on a reference only forbids reassignment, not modification of the object
For real immutability use immutable collections such as List.of

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: What are varargs (e.g., int sum(int... numbers)) and what constraints apply when declaring them?
reference_answer: Varargs allow a method to accept any number of arguments of the same type; inside the method, the varargs parameter is treated as an array. Constraints: each method can have at most one varargs parameter and it must be the LAST parameter. You can call sum(), sum(1), sum(1, 2, 3) or pass an array directly.
key_points: Varargs accept any number of arguments, handled as an array inside
Only one varargs parameter, and it must come last

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: What are wrapper classes such as Integer and Double? What are autoboxing and unboxing?
reference_answer: Wrapper classes are object classes wrapping primitive types (int → Integer, double → Double...), needed because collections and generics only work with objects. Autoboxing is Java automatically converting a primitive to its wrapper object (int → Integer) and unboxing is the reverse, letting you write list.add(5) instead of list.add(Integer.valueOf(5)).
key_points: Wrapper classes box primitives into objects for collections/generics
Autoboxing/unboxing are automatic conversions between primitives and wrappers

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: Why is a String object in Java said to be immutable? What are the benefits?
reference_answer: Once created, a String's content cannot change; methods like toUpperCase() or concat() all return a NEW String. Immutability makes Strings safe to share across threads, enables reuse via the String pool, makes them safe as HashMap keys (the hashCode never changes), and prevents accidental modification when passed as parameters (e.g., file paths, URLs).
key_points: Every 'modifying' operation on a String creates a new String
Benefits: thread safety, String pool, stable HashMap keys, safe sharing

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: Distinguish between a shallow copy and a deep copy of an object.
reference_answer: A shallow copy creates a new object but only copies field values; for reference fields, the copy and the original point to the SAME child objects, so modifying a child object through one affects the other. A deep copy recursively copies child objects as well, producing a structure completely independent of the original.
key_points: Shallow copy: reference fields still share child objects
Deep copy: copies recursively, the copy is fully independent

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: What is unusual about the Cloneable interface in Java compared to ordinary interfaces?
reference_answer: Cloneable is a 'marker interface' — it declares no methods. It only serves as a flag telling Object.clone() that the class allows cloning; calling clone() on an object that does not implement Cloneable throws CloneNotSupportedException. By default, clone() performs a shallow copy.
key_points: Cloneable is a marker interface with no methods
Object.clone() checks for Cloneable and performs a shallow copy by default

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: What are the main methods of the Iterator<T> interface and what is it used for?
reference_answer: Iterator provides a way to traverse the elements of a collection sequentially without knowing its internal structure. Main methods: hasNext() checks whether more elements remain, next() returns the next element, and remove() (optional) safely removes the element most recently returned by next() during iteration.
key_points: Iterator has hasNext(), next(), remove() (optional)
Allows traversing a collection without exposing its internals

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: The Iterable interface and the for-each loop
question: What must a custom class do to be usable in a for-each loop (for (X x : obj))?
reference_answer: The class must implement Iterable<X> and provide an iterator() method returning an Iterator<X>. The compiler translates a for-each loop into a call to iterator() followed by a hasNext()/next() loop, so any class implementing Iterable can use this syntax.
key_points: Implement Iterable<T> and provide iterator()
for-each is compiled into a loop using an Iterator

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: Why should you declare List<String> list = new ArrayList<>(); instead of ArrayList<String> list = new ArrayList<>();?
reference_answer: Declaring the variable by its interface type (List) instead of the concrete implementation (ArrayList) means the rest of the code depends only on the general contract of List. When you need to switch to LinkedList or another implementation, you only change the instantiation point, without affecting the code that uses it. This is the principle 'program to an interface, not an implementation'.
key_points: Declaring by interface makes code depend only on the general contract
Implementations can be swapped without affecting client code

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: What problem does the Abstract Factory Pattern solve?
reference_answer: Abstract Factory provides an interface for creating a FAMILY of related or dependent objects without specifying concrete classes. For example, a GUIFactory with createButton() and createDialog(); WindowsFactory and MacFactory implement it to create components of a consistent style. The client only works with the abstract factory, guaranteeing the created products are always compatible with each other.
key_points: Abstract Factory creates a family of related objects through a common interface
Ensures products of the same family are compatible; client does not depend on concrete classes

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: How does the Prototype Pattern create new objects?
reference_answer: Prototype creates new objects by COPYING (cloning) an existing prototype object instead of calling a constructor and initializing from scratch. It is useful when initialization is expensive (reading configuration, querying data) or when many similar objects are needed, and it lets the client create objects without knowing the concrete class.
key_points: Prototype creates objects by copying a prototype object
Useful when initialization is expensive or many similar objects are needed

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: What does the Iterator Pattern separate from what?
reference_answer: The Iterator Pattern separates HOW to traverse elements from the STORAGE STRUCTURE of the collection. The collection only needs to provide an iterator object; the client traverses through the iterator via a uniform interface (hasNext/next) regardless of whether the underlying storage is an array, a linked list or a tree. This allows changing the storage structure or offering multiple traversal methods without changing client code.
key_points: Separates traversal from internal storage structure
Clients traverse via a uniform interface regardless of the underlying structure

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: How does the Chain of Responsibility Pattern work?
reference_answer: Chain of Responsibility arranges handler objects into a chain; a request is passed along the chain, and each handler either handles it or forwards it to the next handler. The sender does not need to know which handler will process it. Example: an expense approval system going Team Lead → Department Head → Director depending on the amount.
key_points: Handlers are linked into a chain; requests are forwarded along it
Decouples the sender from the specific handler

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: What problem between objects does the Mediator Pattern reduce?
reference_answer: When many objects communicate directly with each other, the links grow like a 'spider web' (n objects can have up to n(n-1) links). Mediator introduces a coordinating intermediary object: objects only communicate with the mediator instead of with each other, reducing coupling between them. For example, an air traffic control tower coordinates aircraft instead of the aircraft contacting each other directly.
key_points: Mediator coordinates communication among many objects
Reduces direct links and coupling between objects

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: Which feature is the Memento Pattern typically used to implement?
reference_answer: Memento allows capturing (snapshotting) the internal state of an object at a point in time and restoring it later without violating encapsulation. It is typically used to implement Undo/Redo, game save points or editor checkpoints. Three roles: Originator (the original object), Memento (the state snapshot), Caretaker (the holder of mementos).
key_points: Memento saves and restores an object's state without breaking encapsulation
Used for Undo/Redo and checkpoints; roles: Originator, Memento, Caretaker

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: Which resource does the Flyweight Pattern save, and how?
reference_answer: Flyweight saves MEMORY when a huge number of similar objects are needed, by SHARING the common part of their state among many objects instead of each object keeping its own copy. For example, a text editor shares font-format objects among millions of identical characters, storing only each character's position separately.
key_points: Flyweight saves memory when there are very many similar objects
Shares common state instead of duplicating it for each object

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: Which two parts of a system does the Bridge Pattern decouple?
reference_answer: Bridge decouples the ABSTRACTION (what the client uses) from the IMPLEMENTATION (how it is concretely done) so the two can evolve independently. For example, a Shape class (Circle, Square) holds a reference to a Renderer interface (OpenGLRenderer, SVGRenderer); adding a new shape or a new rendering method does not require creating every combination of subclasses.
key_points: Bridge separates abstraction from implementation via composition
Both dimensions can be extended independently, avoiding a subclass explosion

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: What three components make up the MVC (Model-View-Controller) pattern and what is the role of each?
reference_answer: The Model holds data and business logic; the View is responsible for displaying data to the user; the Controller receives user actions, asks the Model to process them and selects an appropriate View to display the result. Separating the three roles lets you change the UI without affecting business logic and vice versa.
key_points: Model: data + business logic; View: presentation; Controller: input handling and coordination
Separation allows UI and business logic to change independently

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: What does the Law of Demeter ('only talk to your immediate friends') state?
reference_answer: The Law of Demeter advises that an object's method should only call methods of: itself, its parameters, objects it creates, and its direct components — it should not 'reach through' another object to call further (e.g., avoid order.getCustomer().getAddress().getCity()). The goal is to reduce dependence on other objects' internal structure.
key_points: Only call methods of yourself, parameters, created objects and direct components
Avoid call chains through multiple objects to reduce coupling

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: To which class does the Information Expert principle in GRASP suggest assigning a responsibility?
reference_answer: Information Expert advises assigning a responsibility to the class that HOLDS the information needed to fulfill it. For example, calculating an order's total belongs to the Order class (which holds the list of line items), while calculating each line's subtotal belongs to OrderLine (which has the quantity and unit price).
key_points: Assign a responsibility to the class with enough information to fulfill it
Increases cohesion and reduces passing data back and forth

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: According to GRASP's Creator principle, which class should be responsible for creating objects of class B?
reference_answer: Class A should create B if A contains or aggregates B, records B, closely uses B, or has the initializing data for B. For example, Order should create OrderLines because it contains them. This principle reduces coupling since A is already related to B.
key_points: A should create B if A contains, records, closely uses, or has the initializing data for B
Keeps coupling low because the A-B relationship already exists

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: Which design question does the Controller principle in GRASP answer?
reference_answer: Controller answers: which object (outside the UI layer) should receive and coordinate a system event (e.g., 'place order', 'checkout')? The answer is a controller object representing the whole system or a use case scenario. The controller receives requests from the UI and delegates to domain objects, keeping business logic out of the UI.
key_points: The controller is the first object beyond the UI to receive and coordinate system events
It delegates to domain objects, separating UI from business logic

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: What parts does a CRC card used in object-oriented design consist of?
reference_answer: A CRC card is a small card describing a class with three parts: Class (class name), Responsibilities (what the class knows and does), and Collaborators (other classes it needs to work with to fulfill its responsibilities). CRC cards help a team brainstorm and allocate responsibilities quickly before drawing detailed UML.
key_points: A CRC card has Class, Responsibilities, Collaborators
A lightweight tool for assigning responsibilities in early design

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: What does a UML Sequence Diagram represent?
reference_answer: A Sequence Diagram shows interactions among objects in TIME ORDER for a specific scenario: objects are placed horizontally with lifelines extending downward, messages (method calls) are horizontal arrows between lifelines, and time flows from top to bottom.
key_points: A Sequence Diagram shows object interactions in time order
Elements: lifelines, messages (arrows), time flowing downward

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: What are the basic components of a UML Use Case Diagram?
reference_answer: A Use Case Diagram consists of: Actors (users or external systems interacting with the system), Use Cases (functions the system provides, drawn as ellipses), the system boundary, and relationships among them (association, include, extend, generalization). It describes what the system does from the user's perspective, not how it is implemented.
key_points: Components: Actor, Use Case, system boundary, relationships
Describes functionality from the user's perspective, not implementation

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: What kind of objects is a UML State Machine Diagram suited to describe?
reference_answer: A State Machine Diagram describes the STATES an object can go through during its lifetime and the event-triggered TRANSITIONS between them. It suits objects whose behavior strongly depends on state, e.g., an Order (New → Paid → Shipping → Completed / Cancelled) or a vending machine.
key_points: Describes an object's states and event-driven transitions
Suited to state-dependent objects such as orders

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: In a UML class diagram, what do the symbols +, -, #, ~ before attributes/methods mean?
reference_answer: They indicate visibility: + is public, - is private, # is protected, ~ is package (Java's default). In addition, static members are usually underlined and abstract members are italicized.
key_points: + public, - private, # protected, ~ package
Static is underlined, abstract is italic

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: What do multiplicities like 1, 0..1, 1..*, * on an association between two UML classes mean?
reference_answer: Multiplicity tells how many objects at one end can be linked to an object at the other end: 1 means exactly one, 0..1 means zero or one (optional), 1..* means at least one, * (or 0..*) means zero or many. For example, Customer 1 —— * Order means a customer has many orders and each order belongs to exactly one customer.
key_points: Multiplicity indicates how many objects can be linked at each end
1, 0..1, 1..*, * mean exactly one, optional, at least one, many

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: What is a 'code smell'? Is it a bug?
reference_answer: A code smell is a surface indication in source code that hints at a deeper design problem, e.g., overly long methods, overly large classes, duplicated code, long parameter lists. A code smell is NOT a bug — the program still works correctly — but it makes code hard to understand and maintain and prone to future bugs; it is a signal to consider refactoring.
key_points: A code smell is a sign of a design problem
Not a bug, but it hurts maintainability; a signal to refactor

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: What is refactoring, and what is the most important precondition for doing it?
reference_answer: Refactoring is changing the internal structure of source code to make it easier to understand and maintain WITHOUT changing the program's external behavior. The key precondition is a reliable automated test suite to confirm behavior is unchanged after each small step, and refactoring should be done in small, safe steps.
key_points: Refactoring improves structure without changing external behavior
Requires automated tests and small steps

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: What is a 'God Class' and why is it considered an anti-pattern?
reference_answer: A God Class is a class that takes on too many responsibilities, knows too much and controls too many parts of the system (often thousands of lines and hundreds of methods). It violates SRP, has low cohesion, every change touches it causing conflicts and cascading bugs, and it is hard to test and understand.
key_points: A God Class holds too many responsibilities and too much knowledge
Violates SRP, low cohesion, hard to test and maintain

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: What problem does try-with-resources in Java solve? What condition must an object meet to be used with it?
reference_answer: try-with-resources automatically closes resources (files, database connections, sockets) when the try block ends, whether normally or due to an exception, avoiding resource leaks and verbose finally code. Objects declared in the try's parentheses must implement AutoCloseable (or Closeable) to have a close() method.
key_points: Automatically calls close() when the try block ends, even on exceptions
Resources must implement AutoCloseable

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: What does a sealed class (Java 17) allow you to control in inheritance?
reference_answer: A sealed class allows a class/interface to specify EXACTLY which classes may extend it via the permits clause, e.g., sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square, Triangle. Subclasses must be declared final, sealed or non-sealed. The hierarchy is thus closed and known in advance, enabling the compiler to check exhaustiveness in type-based switches.
key_points: A sealed class restricts the set of permitted subclasses via permits
Subclasses must be final/sealed/non-sealed; supports exhaustive switch checks

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: What information does getClass() return, and how does it differ from the instanceof operator?
reference_answer: getClass() returns a Class object representing the EXACT runtime type of the object. instanceof checks whether an object is an instance of a type OR any of its subclasses. So for a subclass GraduateStudent extends Student, s instanceof Student is true but s.getClass() == Student.class is false.
key_points: getClass() returns the exact runtime type
instanceof accepts subclasses, getClass() compares the exact type

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: What problem is the Optional<T> class (Java 8+) designed to solve?
reference_answer: Optional<T> is a wrapper object that may contain a value or be empty, used mainly as a RETURN TYPE to explicitly express that a result may be absent (e.g., findStudentById() might find nothing). It forces callers to handle the empty case (orElse, orElseThrow, ifPresent, map) instead of receiving null and risking NullPointerException.
key_points: Optional explicitly represents a possibly absent value
Mainly used as a return type to force callers to handle emptiness, reducing NullPointerException

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: What does the syntax if (obj instanceof Student s) { ... } (pattern matching for instanceof) improve over the traditional style?
reference_answer: The traditional way requires a check followed by a manual cast: if (obj instanceof Student) { Student s = (Student) obj; ... }. Pattern matching combines the type check and the declaration of a casted variable in one step: if the condition is true, s automatically has type Student within the block. The code is shorter and avoids casting mistakes from repeating the type name.
key_points: Combines type checking and casting into one step
Reduces repetitive code and manual casting errors

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: Why is it MANDATORY to override hashCode() when you override equals()? What happens if you forget?
reference_answer: Java's contract requires: if a.equals(b) is true then a.hashCode() must equal b.hashCode(). HashMap/HashSet use hashCode first to choose a bucket, then equals to compare within the bucket. If you override only equals but keep the default (identity-based) hashCode, two logically 'equal' objects get different hash codes and land in different buckets: set.add(a); set.contains(b) returns false even though a.equals(b), and a HashSet may contain logically 'duplicate' elements.
key_points: Contract: equal objects must have equal hash codes
Forgetting hashCode makes HashMap/HashSet miss elements and hold logical duplicates

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: Which properties must a correct equals() implementation satisfy according to the Java specification?
reference_answer: equals() must be: (1) Reflexive: x.equals(x) is true; (2) Symmetric: x.equals(y) if and only if y.equals(x); (3) Transitive: x.equals(y) and y.equals(z) imply x.equals(z); (4) Consistent: repeated calls give the same result if the objects do not change; (5) x.equals(null) is always false. A typical implementation: check this == o, check null and type, cast, then compare significant fields (using Objects.equals for nullable fields).
key_points: Five properties: reflexive, symmetric, transitive, consistent, false for null
Standard procedure: check reference, null, type, then compare significant fields

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: A Product class is sorted by code in most cases, but the reporting screen needs to sort by price descending, then by name. How should this be designed?
reference_answer: Make Product implement Comparable<Product> with compareTo by product code — the natural ordering used by default (TreeSet, Collections.sort). For the report, create a separate Comparator without modifying the class: Comparator.comparing(Product::getPrice).reversed().thenComparing(Product::getName). This keeps Product clean, and each special sorting need is encapsulated in its own reusable Comparator.
key_points: Put the most common ordering in Comparable (natural ordering)
Use composed Comparators (comparing, reversed, thenComparing) for special criteria without modifying the class

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: Instead of writing a switch on enum ShippingMethod in many places to compute fees, how can the enum itself be leveraged to eliminate those switches?
reference_answer: An enum in Java is a full class, so it can have fields, constructors and methods, and each constant can even override an abstract method. E.g., enum ShippingMethod { EXPRESS { double fee(double kg) { return 30000 + kg*5000; } }, ECONOMY { ... }; abstract double fee(double kg); }. The fee logic is attached directly to each constant, so adding a new method only requires adding a constant; the compiler forces fee to be implemented, so no switch branch can be forgotten somewhere.
key_points: Enums can contain fields, constructors, methods, and per-constant methods
Attaching behavior to enum constants replaces scattered switches; the compiler ensures completeness

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: Why does Joshua Bloch (Effective Java) recommend implementing a Singleton as an enum with a single constant (enum Config { INSTANCE; ... })?
reference_answer: An enum singleton is guaranteed by the JVM to be initialized exactly once and is thread-safe without manual synchronization. It also automatically resists two common ways of breaking Singletons: serialization/deserialization (Java guarantees enums are not re-created on deserialization) and using reflection to call a private constructor (the JVM forbids instantiating enums via reflection). Drawbacks: it cannot extend another class, and fine-grained lazy initialization is not possible.
key_points: The JVM guarantees one-time initialization and thread safety
Automatically resists serialization and reflection attacks; limitation: cannot extend another class

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: When should you use a record instead of a regular class, and when is a record NOT appropriate?
reference_answer: Records fit pure-data, immutable objects compared by value: DTOs, query results, coordinates, money amounts, composite Map keys. Records are not appropriate when the object needs mutable state (entities with a lifecycle, e.g., an Account whose balance changes), needs to extend another class (records implicitly extend java.lang.Record and are final), needs to hide some fields (every component has a public accessor), or when identity matters more than value.
key_points: Records suit immutable data compared by value (DTOs, value objects)
Not suited for mutable entities, inheritance needs, hidden fields or identity-based objects

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: Choosing an inner class or a static nested class
question: When designing a Node class inside a LinkedList class, should Node be a static nested class or an inner class? Why?
reference_answer: It should be a static nested class. Node only needs to store data and a reference to the next node; it does not need access to the state of a specific LinkedList object. If declared as an inner class, EVERY Node implicitly holds an extra reference to the enclosing list object, wasting memory (one extra pointer per node) and possibly keeping the outer object alive longer than necessary. General rule: default to static nested, and only use an inner class when you truly need access to the enclosing instance.
key_points: Node does not need the list object's state, so make it static nested
An inner class implicitly holds an outer reference, costing memory and extending the outer object's lifetime

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: Differences between lambdas and anonymous classes
question: Besides shorter syntax, how do lambdas differ semantically from anonymous classes?
reference_answer: (1) The this keyword: in an anonymous class, this refers to the anonymous class object itself; in a lambda, this refers to the enclosing class's object. (2) A lambda does not introduce a new scope, so it cannot declare a variable with the same name as an outer local variable, whereas an anonymous class can shadow it. (3) A lambda can only implement a functional interface, while an anonymous class can extend an abstract class or implement an interface with several methods and can have its own state. (4) Lambdas are typically implemented by the JVM via invokedynamic, without generating a separate .class file for each lambda.
key_points: In a lambda, this is the enclosing object; in an anonymous class it is the class itself
Lambdas only target functional interfaces and introduce no new scope; anonymous classes are more flexible and can have state

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: Why can lambdas and anonymous classes only use local variables of the enclosing method that are 'effectively final' (never reassigned after initialization)?
reference_answer: Local variables live on the method's stack and disappear when the method ends, while a lambda may run later (e.g., on another thread). Therefore Java COPIES the variable's value into the lambda at creation time. If reassignment were allowed, the values inside and outside the lambda would diverge, causing confusion and concurrency bugs. The effectively-final rule guarantees the copy is always correct. To share mutable state, use an object field or a holder object such as AtomicInteger.
key_points: Lambdas keep a copy of local variables because stack variables may be gone when the lambda runs
Effectively final keeps the copy consistent; for mutable state use a field or a holder like AtomicInteger

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: There are four kinds of method references in Java. Name them and give an example of each.
reference_answer: (1) Reference to a static method: Integer::parseInt equals s -> Integer.parseInt(s). (2) Reference to a method of a particular object: System.out::println equals x -> System.out.println(x). (3) Reference to an instance method of an arbitrary object of a type: String::toUpperCase equals s -> s.toUpperCase() (the first argument becomes the receiver). (4) Reference to a constructor: ArrayList::new equals () -> new ArrayList<>().
key_points: Four kinds: static, method of a particular object, instance method of an arbitrary object of a type, constructor
A method reference is shorthand for a lambda that only calls an existing method

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: Comparing Abstract Factory and Factory Method
question: Compare Abstract Factory and Factory Method in terms of mechanism and scope of application.
reference_answer: Factory Method relies on INHERITANCE: a superclass defines a creation method and subclasses override it to decide which ONE concrete product to create. Abstract Factory relies on COMPOSITION: the client receives a factory object with SEVERAL creation methods producing a FAMILY of related products (button, dialog, scrollbar of the same style). Factory Method suits deferring the choice of a single product class; Abstract Factory suits guaranteeing that multiple created products are always compatible. In practice, each method in an Abstract Factory is often itself a factory method.
key_points: Factory Method: inheritance, creates one kind of product; Abstract Factory: composition, creates a product family
Abstract Factory guarantees compatibility among products of the same family

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: When implementing Prototype for a Document class containing a List<Page>, what must you watch out for so that the copy does not corrupt the original?
reference_answer: If you only use super.clone() (a shallow copy), the copy and the original share the SAME List<Page> object: adding/removing pages on the copy also changes the original. A deep copy at the appropriate level is needed: create a new List and copy each Page (if Page is mutable). It is often better to use a copy constructor or a custom copy() method instead of Cloneable to clearly control what is shared and what is duplicated.
key_points: Shallow clone() makes the copy and original share mutable collections
Deep-copy mutable components; prefer copy constructors/custom copy methods

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: Why does the code for (Student s : list) { if (s.score < 5) list.remove(s); } usually throw ConcurrentModificationException? What is the correct fix?
reference_answer: Iterators of ArrayList/HashMap are 'fail-fast': they record the structural modification count (modCount) at the start and recheck it on every next(). Calling list.remove() directly changes modCount outside the iterator's control, so the next call to next() detects the anomaly and throws. Fix: use an explicit iterator and call it.remove(), or use list.removeIf(s -> s.score < 5), or collect elements to remove into a separate list and remove them afterwards.
key_points: Fail-fast iterators compare modCount; direct structural modification during iteration is detected
Fix with Iterator.remove(), removeIf(), or removing after iteration

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: Applying Chain of Responsibility to request filters
question: A web server must check, in order: authentication, authorization, rate limiting and logging before handling a request. Analyze applying Chain of Responsibility instead of writing one long method full of ifs.
reference_answer: Each check is encapsulated in its own handler with a common interface (handle(request, next)); each handler either stops the chain (returning 401, 429...) or passes it on. Benefits: each handler has one responsibility (SRP), handlers are easy to test independently, adding/removing/reordering steps only requires reconfiguring the chain (OCP), and chains can be reused across routes. This is exactly the middleware/filter model in Express, Servlet Filters and Spring Security. Note that order matters (e.g., authentication must come before authorization).
key_points: Each check is an independent handler that either stops or forwards
Easy to add/remove/reorder steps and test individually; this is the real-world middleware/filter model

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: Mediator and Observer both reduce coupling between objects. How do they differ?
reference_answer: Observer sets up a one-to-many relationship: the subject broadcasts notifications, observers subscribe themselves; the subject neither knows nor controls what observers do — information flow is distributed. Mediator centralizes interaction logic in a coordinating object that knows all components and decides who does what when an event occurs — control flow is centralized. Observer suits change notification; Mediator suits objects with complex mutual interactions (e.g., interdependent fields in a form). The two often combine: a mediator may use the observer mechanism to receive events.
key_points: Observer: one-to-many broadcast, distributed flow, subject does not control observers
Mediator: centralizes coordination logic in an object that knows all components

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: When implementing Undo for a TextEditor class, why is the Memento designed so that only the Originator can read its contents, not the Caretaker?
reference_answer: The Memento contains internal state (content, cursor position, selection...) that only the TextEditor should know. If the Caretaker (the class managing Undo history) could read/modify the memento, it would depend on the Originator's internal structure and could create invalid states, breaking encapsulation. In Java, a Memento is often implemented as a static nested class with private constructor/getters, or with an empty interface exposed outward (narrow interface) and the full implementation visible only to the Originator (wide interface). The Caretaker just stores and returns the memento as a 'sealed box'.
key_points: The Memento contains internal state that only the Originator should read/write
The Caretaker only holds mementos as sealed boxes (narrow interface) to preserve encapsulation

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: In the Flyweight Pattern, distinguish intrinsic and extrinsic state using the example of a game rendering a forest of one million trees.
reference_answer: Intrinsic state is the SHAREABLE, context-independent part: tree type, 3D model, texture, leaf color — stored in a TreeType flyweight object, of which only a few dozen exist. Extrinsic state depends on each instance: x, y coordinates, size, tilt — stored separately (e.g., in a lightweight array or a Tree object holding only coordinates and a reference to TreeType) and passed in when rendering. Heavy data (textures, meshes) is thus not duplicated a million times. Flyweights must be immutable because they are shared, and are usually obtained through a caching factory.
key_points: Intrinsic: shared, context-independent part stored in the flyweight
Extrinsic: per-instance part passed in when used; flyweights must be immutable and obtained via a caching factory

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: Bridge and Adapter both use composition to connect two parts. How do they differ?
reference_answer: They differ mainly in INTENT and TIMING: Adapter is an 'after the fact' solution — making an existing class with an incompatible interface work with existing code (e.g., wrapping a third-party payment library). Bridge is an 'up-front' design decision — deliberately separating abstraction and implementation so both dimensions can evolve independently (e.g., Notification × Channel: Email, SMS, Push). Adapter usually wraps one object to change its interface; Bridge designs two parallel hierarchies connected by a reference.
key_points: Adapter: reconciles incompatible interfaces of existing components (retrofit)
Bridge: proactively separates two varying dimensions so they extend independently

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: Briefly compare MVC, MVP and MVVM in terms of how the View relates to presentation logic.
reference_answer: MVC: the Controller handles input and updates the Model; the View reads/observes the Model to display it, and View and Model may know each other. MVP: the Presenter sits fully in between, the View is passive, only displaying and forwarding events to the Presenter through an interface; the Presenter updates the View explicitly — easy to test because the View can be mocked. MVVM: the ViewModel exposes state and commands, and the View binds to it via two-way data binding, so there is almost no manual UI-update code; the ViewModel does not know the View. The general trend is to separate the View from logic more and more to improve testability.
key_points: MVC: View observes the Model; MVP: Presenter drives a passive View through an interface
MVVM: View binds to the ViewModel, which does not know the View; the goal is testable separation of logic and UI

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: Fixing a Law of Demeter violation (Train Wreck)
question: The code if (order.getCustomer().getWallet().getBalance() >= total) order.getCustomer().getWallet().deduct(total); violates what, and how should it be fixed?
reference_answer: This is a 'train wreck' violating the Law of Demeter: the caller must know Customer's internal structure (it has a Wallet) and Wallet's (it has a balance), coupling it to the whole chain of classes; if the wallet storage changes (multiple wallets, reward points), every caller must change. Also, the check-then-deduct logic is in the wrong place. Move the behavior to where the data is (Tell, Don't Ask): customer.pay(total) — inside, Customer delegates to wallet.deduct(amount), and Wallet checks its own balance and throws an exception if insufficient.
key_points: Getter chains across objects couple the caller to the internals of many classes
Fix by moving behavior to the object owning the data and delegating layer by layer

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: What is the Pure Fabrication principle in GRASP? Give an example.
reference_answer: Sometimes assigning responsibility by Information Expert lowers cohesion or increases coupling — e.g., putting the job of saving an Order to the database into the Order class makes the domain class depend on JDBC/SQL. Pure Fabrication advises creating an 'artificial' class that does not correspond to any domain concept, solely to carry that responsibility with high cohesion, e.g., OrderRepository, EmailSenderService, CurrencyConverter. Most services, repositories and adapters in practice are pure fabrications.
key_points: Pure Fabrication: create a class not in the domain model to carry a technical responsibility
Keeps domain classes highly cohesive and loosely coupled; e.g., Repository, Service

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: Explain the relationship between the Indirection and Protected Variations principles in GRASP.
reference_answer: Protected Variations is the GOAL: identify points likely to change or be unstable (payment providers, file formats, tax algorithms) and protect the rest of the system from those changes with a stable interface. Indirection is the MEANS: place an intermediary object between two components so they do not depend directly on each other (adapter, gateway, interface). Most design patterns (Adapter, Facade, Strategy, Observer) are ways of applying Indirection to achieve Protected Variations.
key_points: Protected Variations: shield the system from points of variation with stable interfaces
Indirection: use intermediaries to remove direct dependencies — the means to that goal

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: The method calculateSalary(Employee e) has switch(e.getType()) with branches FULLTIME, PARTTIME, INTERN, and similar switches appear in calculateBonus() and printPayslip(). Propose a suitable refactoring.
reference_answer: Apply 'Replace Conditional with Polymorphism': create an Employee superclass/interface with abstract methods calculateSalary(), calculateBonus(); each type becomes a subclass (FullTimeEmployee, PartTimeEmployee, Intern) implementing them. Adding a new employee type then only requires a new subclass instead of hunting down every switch (satisfying OCP, removing the 'repeated switch' smell). If an employee's type can change during the object's lifetime, use State/Strategy (composition) instead of subclasses.
key_points: Repeated switches on a type code are a code smell
Replace with polymorphism: each type is a subclass implementing its behavior; use Strategy/State if the type changes at runtime

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: Data Clumps and Introduce Parameter Object
question: Many methods take the same parameter set (startDate, endDate), like findOrders(startDate, endDate), calculateRevenue(startDate, endDate). What code smell is this and how should it be refactored?
reference_answer: This is 'Data Clumps' — a group of data that always travels together but has not been turned into a concept. Refactor with 'Introduce Parameter Object': create a DateRange class/record(startDate, endDate). Benefits: shorter parameter lists, the invariant (startDate <= endDate) is checked once in the constructor, and there is a home for related behavior such as contains(date), overlaps(other), days() instead of repeating it in many places.
key_points: Data Clumps: parameters that always travel together but are not yet a concept
Introduce Parameter Object groups them into a class, centralizing invariant checks and attracting related behavior

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: A Customer class stores email, phoneNumber and amount all as String/double, and format validation is scattered across the system. Analyze the code smell and how to fix it.
reference_answer: This is 'Primitive Obsession' — using primitive types to represent domain concepts with their own rules. Consequences: validation is duplicated or forgotten, parameters are easily swapped (two Strings swapped still compile), and double for money causes rounding errors. Fix with immutable Value Objects: Email, PhoneNumber, Money(amount BigDecimal, currency) — the constructor validates so every existing object is valid, equality is by value, and the compiler distinguishes the types.
key_points: Primitive Obsession: using primitives for domain concepts with rules
Replace with immutable, self-validating Value Objects: type-safe and precise (BigDecimal for money)

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: Distinguish the code smells 'Shotgun Surgery' and 'Divergent Change'.
reference_answer: Divergent Change: ONE class is modified for MANY different reasons (changing the database modifies it, changing the report format also modifies it) — a sign the class has multiple responsibilities and should be split (Extract Class). Shotgun Surgery is the opposite: ONE small change forces edits in MANY different classes (changing the tax calculation touches 8 files) — a sign a responsibility is scattered and should be consolidated (Move Method/Move Field). Both relate to poorly allocated responsibilities.
key_points: Divergent Change: one class changes for many reasons; split the class
Shotgun Surgery: one change spreads across many classes; consolidate the responsibility

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: An Employee class has fields name, salary, houseNumber, street, ward, city, postalCode and address-formatting methods. Analyze and propose a refactoring.
reference_answer: The address fields and address-formatting methods form a separate responsibility, highly cohesive with each other but weakly cohesive with the rest of Employee. Apply Extract Class: create an Address class (ideally an immutable value object) holding the fields and formatting behavior, with Employee keeping an Address reference. Result: Employee is leaner, Address is reusable for Customer and Supplier, and changes to address rules affect only one class.
key_points: Groups of tightly related fields and behavior are candidates for extraction
Extract Class creates a reusable Address, reducing size and increasing cohesion of Employee

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: What is the 'Middle Man' code smell? Does it contradict the advice to use delegation to follow the Law of Demeter?
reference_answer: A Middle Man is a class whose methods mostly just forward calls to another object without adding value. It is the flip side of over-applying the Law of Demeter: to avoid getter chains, too many 'pass-through' delegating methods are added. Balance is needed: delegation is meaningful when it hides details and expresses business behavior; if a class does nothing but delegate, remove the middle man (Remove Middle Man) so clients work directly with the real object, or revisit the allocation of responsibilities.
key_points: Middle Man: a class that mainly forwards calls without adding value
It results from over-applying Demeter; balance hiding details against empty intermediaries

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: In try-with-resources, if the try block throws exception A and then the resource's close() throws exception B, which exception propagates? Where does the other one go?
reference_answer: Exception A (from the try block) is the primary exception propagated, since it usually reflects the root cause. Exception B from close() is not lost but attached to A as a 'suppressed exception', retrievable via A.getSuppressed(). This is a big improvement over manual try-finally, where an exception thrown in finally overwrites and loses the original exception.
key_points: The exception from the try block takes priority and propagates
The close() exception is stored as suppressed (getSuppressed()), not lost as with a manual finally

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: Why should the service layer not let SQLException from the data access layer propagate straight up to the UI layer? How should it be handled?
reference_answer: SQLException is an implementation detail of the data layer; letting it propagate makes upper layers depend on the storage technology (switching to NoSQL or an API means changing every place that catches SQLException) and breaks abstraction. Apply 'exception translation': the lower layer catches low-level exceptions and throws exceptions appropriate to its own abstraction level (e.g., OrderNotFoundException, StorageException), while keeping the original as the cause (exception chaining) to preserve debugging information.
key_points: Low-level exceptions leaking upward expose implementation details and increase coupling between layers
Translate to exceptions at the right abstraction level, keeping the original as the cause

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: Compare three ways of injecting dependencies: via constructor, via setter and via field (e.g., @Autowired on a field).
reference_answer: Constructor injection: dependencies are passed at creation, can be final, the object is always valid, dependencies are visible in the signature, and it is easy to test by passing mocks — the recommended way for required dependencies. Setter injection: suits optional or changeable dependencies, but the object may exist without all its dependencies. Field injection: concise but hides dependencies, cannot be final, is hard to test outside the container (requires reflection), and conceals that a class has too many dependencies.
key_points: Constructor injection: required, immutable, explicit, easy to test — preferred
Setter for optional dependencies; field injection is concise but hides dependencies and is hard to test

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: Service Locator (a global lookup class: ServiceLocator.get(EmailService.class)) and Dependency Injection both decouple from concrete classes. Why is DI generally preferred?
reference_answer: With a Service Locator, a class 'pulls' its dependencies from a global registry inside method bodies, so dependencies are hidden — looking at the constructor signature does not reveal what the class needs; tests must configure the global registry, easily causing cross-test interference; and the class depends on the ServiceLocator itself. With DI, dependencies are 'pushed' in from outside, declared explicitly in the constructor, and easily replaced by mocks. Service Locator still has uses at system boundaries or in hard-to-change legacy code.
key_points: Service Locator hides dependencies and ties the class to a global registry
DI declares dependencies explicitly and is easy to test; preferred in most cases

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: What role does the Repository Pattern play in domain-driven design, and in which layer should its interface live?
reference_answer: A Repository acts like an 'in-memory collection of domain objects' (addOrder, findById, findUnpaidOrders), completely hiding storage details (SQL, ORM, API). The repository interface should live in the domain layer and be expressed in business language, while the implementation (JpaOrderRepository) lives in the infrastructure layer — applying DIP: the domain layer does not depend on infrastructure, but the other way around.
key_points: A Repository hides storage behind a collection-like interface of domain objects
Interface in the domain layer, implementation in infrastructure (applying DIP)

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: Static and private methods in interfaces
question: Since Java 8/9, interfaces can have static methods and private methods. What is each used for?
reference_answer: Static methods in interfaces provide utility or factory methods tied to that interface (e.g., Comparator.comparing(), List.of()), instead of needing a companion utility class like Collections; they are not inherited by implementing classes and are called via the interface name. Private methods (Java 9) let default or static methods inside the interface share code without exposing it as part of the API.
key_points: Static methods: utilities/factories tied to the interface, called via the interface name
Private methods: share code among default/static methods without exposing it in the API

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: Reading Sequence Diagrams: synchronous and asynchronous messages
question: In a Sequence Diagram, distinguish synchronous messages, asynchronous messages and return messages; what does an activation bar represent?
reference_answer: A synchronous message (filled arrowhead) means the sender waits for the receiver to finish before continuing — corresponding to a normal method call. An asynchronous message (open arrowhead) means the sender continues immediately without waiting — like sending an event or pushing to a queue. A return message is a dashed arrow back to the caller. An activation bar (narrow rectangle on a lifeline) represents the period during which an object is executing an operation, making nested calls visible.
key_points: Synchronous: filled arrowhead, waits for result; asynchronous: open arrowhead, no waiting; return: dashed
The activation bar shows the time an object is processing

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: Include and extend relationships in Use Cases
question: Distinguish <<include>> and <<extend>> relationships between use cases, with examples.
reference_answer: <<include>>: the base use case ALWAYS includes the behavior of the included use case; used to factor out shared parts — e.g., both 'Place order' and 'Cancel order' include 'Log in'. The arrow goes from the base use case to the included one. <<extend>>: the extending use case is added to the base use case only under certain conditions (optional) — e.g., 'Apply discount code' extends 'Checkout'. The arrow goes from the extending use case to the base use case.
key_points: include: mandatory behavior, always performed, factors out shared parts
extend: optional, conditional behavior; arrow from the extending use case to the base

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: From a State Machine Diagram to the State Pattern
question: Given a State Machine Diagram for Order with states New, Paid, Shipping, Completed, Cancelled, describe how to turn it into code using the State Pattern.
reference_answer: Each state in the diagram becomes a class implementing an OrderState interface, and the events on transition arrows become interface methods (pay(), ship(), confirmReceipt(), cancel()). In each state class, the method for a valid transition performs the action and sets the new state on the Order (context); an event invalid in that state throws an exception. The Order holds a reference to the current state and delegates every call to it. The code thus directly mirrors the diagram and eliminates state-based if-else chains.
key_points: States → classes implementing an interface; transition events → methods
The context delegates to the current state; invalid transitions throw, removing if-else chains

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: What is the Object Pool Pattern and why is a connection pool in database applications a classic example?
reference_answer: An Object Pool keeps a set of pre-initialized objects for reuse: clients 'borrow' an object from the pool and 'return' it when done instead of creating and destroying objects. It pays off when object creation is expensive and concurrency must be limited. Database connections are the classic example because opening a connection is slow (network handshake, authentication) and the database can only handle a limited number of connections. Caveats: reset the object's state when returning it and always return it (use try-with-resources) to avoid exhausting the pool.
key_points: Object Pool reuses expensive objects instead of constantly creating/destroying them
Connection pools are the classic example; reset state and always return objects to the pool

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: Compare Collections.unmodifiableList(list) and List.copyOf(list) when returning an internal list from a getter.
reference_answer: Collections.unmodifiableList(list) returns a read-only 'view' wrapping the original list: clients cannot modify it through the view, but if the owning object modifies list, clients still see the changes (the view reflects live data), with no copying cost. List.copyOf(list) creates an independent immutable copy at call time: unaffected by later changes, but costs O(n) to copy and does not accept null elements. Choose a view when clients should see updates and to save cost; choose a copy when a stable snapshot is needed (e.g., to iterate on another thread).
key_points: unmodifiableList: read-only view reflecting changes to the original, no copying cost
List.copyOf: independent immutable copy, O(n), no nulls

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: Cost of string concatenation and StringBuilder
question: Why can concatenating strings with += in a loop tens of thousands of times be very slow? How does StringBuilder fix this?
reference_answer: Because String is immutable, each s += x creates a NEW String object and copies the entire old content plus the new part, so n concatenations with growing length cost O(n²) copying in total and create a lot of garbage for the GC. StringBuilder is a mutable object with an expandable buffer (doubling when full); append just writes at the end with amortized O(1) cost, and toString() is called once at the end — O(n) total.
key_points: String is immutable so += in a loop creates many new objects, O(n²) total
StringBuilder is mutable with a growable buffer, amortized O(1) append, O(n) total

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: Comparing Integers with == and the Integer cache
question: Why does Integer a = 100, b = 100; a == b give true, while Integer c = 1000, d = 1000; c == d gives false?
reference_answer: Autoboxing uses Integer.valueOf(), which returns CACHED objects for values in the range -128 to 127. So a and b refer to the same cached object and == (reference comparison) returns true. 1000 is outside the cache range, so each boxing creates a new object; c and d are different objects and == returns false. Lesson: always use equals() to compare the values of wrapper objects.
key_points: Integer.valueOf caches objects for values -128..127
== compares references so the result depends on the cache; always use equals for wrappers

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: Type inference and the diamond operator
question: How do the diamond operator (Map<String, List<Integer>> m = new HashMap<>();) and type inference help? Are there limitations?
reference_answer: The diamond lets the compiler infer the constructor's type arguments from the declared type on the left, avoiding verbose repetition. Similarly, for generic methods like Collections.emptyList(), T is inferred from context. Limitation: inference relies on the target type, so in some complex expressions (call chains, arguments to overloaded methods) the compiler may infer an unintended type (e.g., Object) and you need an explicit type such as Collections.<String>emptyList(). With 'var', be careful: var x = new ArrayList<>() infers ArrayList<Object>.
key_points: Diamond and type inference avoid verbose type repetition
Inference depends on the target context and sometimes needs explicit types; var with diamond yields Object

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: Raw types (using List instead of List<String>) are still accepted by Java. Why should they be avoided?
reference_answer: Raw types exist only for backward compatibility with pre-Java 5 code. With raw types, the compiler disables generic type checking: you can add an Integer to a List meant to hold only Strings without a compile error, and the bug only surfaces at runtime as a ClassCastException far from where it was introduced. Raw types also spread: assigning List<String> to a raw List and back yields unchecked warnings. If you truly do not know the element type, use the wildcard List<?> to keep type safety.
key_points: Raw types disable generic type checks; bugs surface only at runtime (ClassCastException)
They exist only for backward compatibility; use List<?> when the type is unknown

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: Explain the meaning of static <T extends Comparable<T>> T findMax(List<T> list) and why we do not simply write <T extends Comparable>.
reference_answer: The declaration requires T to be comparable with ITSELF (e.g., String implements Comparable<String>), so inside the method a.compareTo(b) can be called type-safely with a and b both of type T. Writing <T extends Comparable> (a raw type) loses the information about what is being compared, produces unchecked warnings and allows comparing incompatible types, failing only at runtime. An even more general version is <T extends Comparable<? super T>>, which also accepts subclasses that inherit compareTo from a superclass.
key_points: T extends Comparable<T> guarantees T is comparable with itself, making compareTo type-safe
Raw Comparable loses type checking; the more general form is Comparable<? super T>

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: Sealed classes combined with switch pattern matching
question: With sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Rectangle and corresponding records, what advantage does a pattern-matching switch for computing area have over a chain of if-instanceof?
reference_answer: Because the set of subclasses is closed and known to the compiler, a switch expression (case Circle c -> PI*c.r()*c.r(); case Rectangle r -> r.w()*r.h();) is checked for exhaustiveness: no default branch is needed, and when a new subclass is added to permits, every switch that does not handle it produces a COMPILE ERROR instead of silently falling into a default branch. An if-instanceof chain has no such check and cases are easily forgotten. This 'algebraic data type' approach replaces Visitor when the set of types is stable.
key_points: Sealed + pattern switch is checked for exhaustiveness by the compiler, no default needed
Adding a new subclass causes compile errors in unhandled switches, safer than if-instanceof

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: Distinguish the test doubles Stub, Mock and Fake when testing an OrderService that depends on a PaymentGateway.
reference_answer: Stub: a stand-in returning canned data (always 'payment succeeded') to put the class under test into a scenario; the test checks STATE/results. Mock: an object programmed with expectations about INTERACTIONS; the test verifies which methods were called, how many times and with what arguments (e.g., verify gateway.charge(500000) was called exactly once). Fake: a working but simplified implementation, e.g., a repository stored in a HashMap instead of a real database. This substitutability is possible because OrderService depends on an interface (DIP).
key_points: Stubs return canned data and check state; mocks verify interactions (what was called, how often)
Fakes are simplified working implementations (in-memory DB); all rely on dependencies via interfaces

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: What three components make up Design by Contract? Apply them to the method withdraw(amount) of an Account class.
reference_answer: Three components: Precondition — what the caller must guarantee before calling: amount > 0 and amount <= balance. Postcondition — what the method guarantees afterwards: new balance = old balance - amount. Class invariant — what is always true for every object in a stable state: balance >= 0. Contracts clearly divide responsibilities between caller and callee and relate directly to LSP: subclasses must not strengthen preconditions or weaken postconditions.
key_points: Three components: precondition, postcondition, class invariant
Divides responsibility between caller and callee; related to LSP

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: Why should parameters be validated at the very start of a constructor (e.g., Objects.requireNonNull(email), checking age >= 0) instead of letting errors appear later when the object is used?
reference_answer: The fail-fast principle: detect invalid data as early as possible, at the point it enters the system. If an object can be created with a null email, a NullPointerException might only occur hours later in another module (when sending mail), making the origin very hard to trace. Validating in the constructor ensures every existing object satisfies its invariants, gives clear error messages pointing at the real culprit, and spares other methods from re-checking.
key_points: Fail-fast detects errors at the point data enters the system
Ensures every object is valid, errors are traceable, and repeated checks are avoided

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: In UI programming, the listener mechanism (e.g., button.addActionListener(...)) applies which pattern and what does it decouple?
reference_answer: A listener is a form of the Observer Pattern combined with callbacks: the button (subject) does not know what will happen when clicked; application code registers an object implementing the listener interface, and the button calls back the listener's method when the event occurs. This decouples a reusable UI component (a library Button) from specific application logic and allows multiple listeners to react to one event. This mechanism is also the foundation of event-driven programming.
key_points: A listener is Observer plus callbacks: the component calls back registered objects on events
Decouples reusable UI components from application logic and allows multiple listeners

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: Package by feature vs package by layer
question: Compare organizing packages by layer (controller/, service/, repository/) versus by feature (order/, customer/, payment/).
reference_answer: Package by layer groups classes with the same technical role together; easy to understand in small projects, but a feature is scattered across packages and most classes must be public for layers to call each other, losing package-level encapsulation. Package by feature groups all classes of a feature in one package: changing a feature touches only one place, package-private can hide details inside the feature exposing only a few public classes, the structure reflects the business, and it is easier to split into modules/microservices later. For medium and large systems, package by feature usually yields higher cohesion.
key_points: By layer: grouped by technical role, features scattered, many public classes
By feature: grouped by business capability, high cohesion, leverages package-private, easier to modularize

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: Violating equals() symmetry when a subclass adds a field
question: Class Point(x, y) has an equals() using instanceof. Subclass ColorPoint(x, y, color) overrides equals() to also compare color, again using instanceof. Analyze why this design violates the equals() contract and the possible solutions.
reference_answer: With p = Point(1,2) and q = ColorPoint(1,2,Red): p.equals(q) returns true (q instanceof Point, coordinates equal) but q.equals(p) returns false (p is not a ColorPoint) — symmetry is violated. If ColorPoint is patched to ignore color when comparing with a plain Point, transitivity breaks instead (Red ColorPoint = Point = Blue ColorPoint but Red ≠ Blue). In fact there is no way to extend an instantiable class with a value field while keeping the equals contract using instanceof. Solutions: (1) prefer composition — ColorPoint contains a Point and offers an asPoint() view instead of inheriting; (2) use getClass() != o.getClass() so objects are equal only if they have exactly the same class (but this breaks LSP, as subclasses cannot substitute the superclass in collections); (3) declare Point final/a record.
key_points: Two-way instanceof with an extra subclass field breaks symmetry; patching it breaks transitivity
Solutions: composition over inheritance, getClass() (trading off LSP), or a final class/record

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: A Student object whose hashCode() is computed from its email field is used as a HashMap key. After put, the program calls s.setEmail(newEmail). Analyze the consequences and the design principle to draw.
reference_answer: The object was stored in the bucket matching its OLD hashCode. After the email changes, the new hashCode differs, so map.get(s) or map.containsKey(s) looks in the new bucket and finds nothing — the entry becomes an 'orphan': it cannot be retrieved or removed via remove(s), it still occupies memory (a form of logical memory leak), and a 'duplicate' entry for the same object can be added. Principle: fields participating in equals/hashCode of objects used as keys (or HashSet elements) must be immutable; ideally use an immutable value object (an ID, a record) as the key instead of a whole mutable entity.
key_points: Changing a hashCode field after put leaves the entry in the wrong bucket, unfindable and unremovable
Keys of HashMap/elements of HashSet must be immutable in the fields used by equals/hashCode

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: Does public int hashCode() { return 42; } violate the equals/hashCode contract? Analyze its impact.
reference_answer: It does not violate the contract: equal objects still have equal hash codes (every object has hash code 42). However, all elements fall into the SAME bucket, turning the HashMap into a linked list (or a red-black tree since Java 8 when the bucket grows), so get/put degrade from average O(1) to O(n) (or O(log n) if keys are Comparable). With hundreds of thousands of elements, performance collapses severely with no error reported. Lesson: the contract only ensures correctness; the distribution quality of hashCode determines performance. Use Objects.hash(...) or combine significant fields with prime multipliers.
key_points: A constant does not break the contract but puts all elements in one bucket
HashMap degrades from O(1) to O(n)/O(log n); performance depends on hashCode distribution

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: new BigDecimal("1.0").equals(new BigDecimal("1.00")) is false but compareTo returns 0. Analyze the consequences of adding both values to a HashSet and a TreeSet.
reference_answer: HashSet uses equals/hashCode, so it treats 1.0 and 1.00 as two different elements: size 2.
