TreeSet uses compareTo (or a Comparator) to detect duplicates, so it treats them as equal: size 1. The same data in two 'Set' structures yields different results, violating the expectations of the Set interface (which is defined in terms of equals). Lesson: when compareTo is inconsistent with equals, document it clearly, and when writing a Comparator for TreeSet/TreeMap make sure it returns 0 only when two objects really are duplicates; otherwise elements are silently dropped (e.g., a Comparator comparing only by score loses students with the same score).
key_points: HashSet uses equals, TreeSet uses compareTo, so results differ when the two are inconsistent
A Comparator returning 0 for distinct objects makes TreeSet/TreeMap silently drop elements

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: The comparator (a, b) -> a.getId() - b.getId() with int ids looks neat. Analyze the hidden bug.
reference_answer: Subtracting two ints can OVERFLOW when the values have opposite signs and large magnitudes: e.g., a = Integer.MAX_VALUE, b = -1, then a - b overflows to a negative number and the Comparator concludes a < b — wrong. The result is an inconsistent ordering that violates the Comparator contract (transitivity), which can make TimSort throw 'Comparison method violates its general contract' or TreeMap place elements wrongly, and the bug only shows up for special data. Correct way: Integer.compare(a.getId(), b.getId()) or Comparator.comparingInt(X::getId).
key_points: a - b can overflow int and flip the sign of the comparison
Violates the contract, causing wrong ordering or exceptions; use Integer.compare/Comparator.comparingInt

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: Memory leak via implicit references in inner classes
question: A ReportScreen class (holding many MB of data) creates a non-static inner class BackgroundTask implements Runnable and submits it to a long-lived thread pool. Analyze the memory leak risk.
reference_answer: Every inner class object implicitly holds a reference to its enclosing object (ReportScreen.this). As long as BackgroundTask sits in the queue or runs in the thread pool (or is stored in a static list or a long-lived registered callback), the ReportScreen object and all its heavy data cannot be garbage collected, even after the screen is closed. This is a classic leak (e.g., an Android Activity held by a Handler/AsyncTask). Fix: use a static nested class and pass in only the data needed, or hold a weak reference (WeakReference) to the outer object, and cancel the task when the outer object's lifecycle ends.
key_points: Inner classes/lambdas using this implicitly retain the enclosing object, preventing GC
Use static nested classes, pass only needed data, WeakReference, and cancel tasks with the lifecycle

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: Unregistering a lambda listener does not work
question: Code registers source.addListener(e -> handle(e)); and later unregisters with source.removeListener(e -> handle(e));. Why is the listener never removed, and what are the consequences?
reference_answer: Each evaluation of a lambda expression (capturing this) may create a NEW object; two identically written lambdas are not equal under equals (lambdas do not override equals, comparing by identity). removeListener searches by equals so it cannot find the registered lambda, and the old listener stays in the list. Consequences: events keep being handled unintentionally (handled twice), and the listener holds a reference to this so the object is never collected — a memory leak. Correct approach: store the listener reference in a field when registering (Listener l = this::handle;) and use that same reference to unregister, or have addListener return a handle/Subscription with a cancel() method.
key_points: Two lambdas with the same code are distinct objects and not equal under equals
Keep the exact registered reference or use an unsubscribe handle; otherwise duplicate handling and memory leaks

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: Analyze the bug in the following lazy Singleton using double-checked locking: if (instance == null) { synchronized (X.class) { if (instance == null) instance = new X(); } } return instance; where instance is not declared volatile.
reference_answer: The statement instance = new X() is not atomic: it consists of allocating memory, running the constructor and assigning the reference. The compiler/CPU may reorder these so the reference is assigned BEFORE the constructor finishes. Another thread performing the first check instance == null outside the synchronized block (with no happens-before relationship) may see a non-null instance and use a partially constructed object — fields still holding default values, causing extremely hard-to-reproduce bugs. Fix: declare private static volatile X instance (volatile forbids the reordering and establishes happens-before), or use the holder idiom (a static nested class holding the instance; the JVM guarantees safe class initialization), or an enum singleton.
key_points: Without volatile, the reference assignment may be reordered before the constructor completes
Other threads may see a half-constructed object; fix with volatile, the holder idiom or an enum

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: Breaking a Singleton via serialization, reflection and cloning
question: A classic Singleton (private constructor, static getInstance()) implements Serializable. Analyze three ways a second instance can be created and how to defend against them.
reference_answer: (1) Serialization: deserialization always creates a new object without calling the constructor; defend by implementing readResolve() returning the single instance (and marking fields transient). (2) Reflection: setAccessible(true) on the private constructor and then newInstance(); defend by throwing an exception in the constructor if the instance already exists (which can still be bypassed if reflection runs before the first initialization). (3) Cloning: if the class (or a superclass) supports clone, it can be duplicated; defend by overriding clone() to throw CloneNotSupportedException. The thorough solution is an enum singleton, which the JVM protects against all three.
key_points: Three holes: deserialization, reflection on the private constructor, clone()
Defend with readResolve, a constructor check, blocking clone; most robust is an enum singleton

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: Why do many experts consider Java's Cloneable/clone() mechanism a flawed design and recommend copy constructors instead?
reference_answer: (1) Cloneable does not declare clone(), so clone() cannot be called through the interface type; clone() is protected in Object. (2) Object.clone() creates an object WITHOUT calling a constructor, bypassing every invariant check in the constructor. (3) It is shallow by default, so the class must deep-copy mutable fields itself, but final fields cannot be reassigned in clone(), conflicting with making the class immutable. (4) It requires handling the checked CloneNotSupportedException and casting the result. (5) Subclasses inherit the obligation to clone correctly and easily forget it. A copy constructor (new Document(original)) or a static factory copyOf() is clearer, goes through the constructor, works with final and needs no casting.
key_points: clone() bypasses the constructor, is shallow, conflicts with final fields, and has an awkward API
Copy constructors/static factories are clear, preserve invariants and work with final

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: The code Object[] arr = new String[3]; arr[0] = 10; compiles but fails at runtime, whereas List<Object> l = new ArrayList<String>(); fails to compile. Analyze this design difference.
reference_answer: Arrays in Java are covariant: String[] is a subtype of Object[], so the assignment compiles. But arrays store their actual element type at runtime (reified), so when an Integer is assigned into a String array, the JVM checks and throws ArrayStoreException — the error is only detected at runtime. Generics are invariant: List<String> is not a subtype of List<Object>, so the compiler blocks it immediately, because if allowed, an Integer could be added to a list of Strings without the runtime noticing (due to type erasure). This is why generic arrays (new T[] or new List<String>[]) cannot be created and why List should be preferred over arrays in generic APIs.
key_points: Arrays are covariant and reified: type errors are only detected at runtime via ArrayStoreException
Generics are invariant and erased, so the compiler must block early; generic arrays cannot be created

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: The method static <T> T[] toArray(T... items) { return items; } is called from another generic method. Analyze the risk of 'heap pollution' and the role of @SafeVarargs.
reference_answer: Varargs are implemented with arrays, and an array of a generic type T is erased to Object[] (or the upper bound). If toArray is called from another generic context, the actual array created has type Object[]; returning it and assigning it to a String[] throws a ClassCastException at a seemingly harmless place. Heap pollution is when a variable of a parameterized type refers to an object that is not of that type. @SafeVarargs is merely the author's promise that the method does not write to the varargs array and does not let the array reference escape; it suppresses warnings but does NOT make the method safe — toArray above is precisely an example that must not be annotated @SafeVarargs.
key_points: Generic varargs create erased arrays; letting the array escape causes hard-to-trace ClassCastExceptions
@SafeVarargs is only a promise not to write to or leak the array; it does not make code safe

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: Given Map<String, Integer> stock; both int qty = stock.get(code); and Integer result = condition ? stock.get(code) : 0; can throw NullPointerException. Explain the mechanism.
reference_answer: Case 1: get() returns null when the key is absent; assigning null to an int forces auto-unboxing to call null.intValue() → NPE. Case 2 is subtler: the ternary operator has one branch of type Integer and one of type int, and Java's typing rules choose int as the result type, so the Integer branch is unboxed BEFORE being assigned back to Integer result — if get() returns null, an NPE occurs even though the target is an Integer. Prevention: use getOrDefault(code, 0), check null explicitly, or make both branches Integer (Integer.valueOf(0)).
key_points: Assigning null to a primitive triggers unboxing of null → NPE
A ternary mixing Integer and int forces implicit unboxing; use getOrDefault or unify the types

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: Read-only views still leak changes and lifetime
question: A Classroom class returns Collections.unmodifiableList(students) to clients. A reporting thread iterates this list while Classroom adds new students. Analyze the hidden problems.
reference_answer: (1) A read-only view still reflects changes to the original list; when Classroom modifies the original list while another thread iterates the view, the fail-fast iterator may throw ConcurrentModificationException, or worse, read an inconsistent state because ArrayList is not thread-safe. (2) Unmodifiable applies only to the list itself: the Student objects inside are still mutable, so clients can call s.setScore(...) — shallow encapsulation. (3) Clients may keep the view for a long time, unintentionally retaining all the live data. Solutions depending on needs: return a List.copyOf snapshot for a stable view, use CopyOnWriteArrayList for read-mostly workloads, and use immutable elements or DTOs.
key_points: Read-only views are still affected by changes to the original, causing concurrency bugs
They protect only the list, not mutable elements; consider copies, CopyOnWrite and immutable elements

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: The constructor of a Sensor class calls eventBus.register(this) before all fields are assigned. Analyze the risk in a multi-threaded environment.
reference_answer: When this is published before the constructor completes, another thread (e.g., the event dispatch thread) may call the object's methods while fields are not yet assigned — seeing default null/0 values — causing NPEs or wrong behavior. Even final fields are NOT guaranteed to be correctly visible to other threads if this escapes during construction (the final-field guarantee only applies when the constructor finishes without leaking this). If the class has subclasses, the subclass fields are not yet initialized either. Fix: do not register in the constructor; use a static factory that creates a fully constructed object and then registers it (Sensor s = new Sensor(...); bus.register(s); return s;).
key_points: Publishing this in the constructor lets other threads see a half-built object
It also loses the visibility guarantee of final fields; use a static factory that registers after construction

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: An immutable class that is not final can be broken by subclasses
question: A Money class has private final fields and no setters, but is not declared final. Analyze how a subclass can break its immutability and the security implications.
reference_answer: A subclass can add mutable fields and override methods (getAmount(), toString(), equals) to return values that change over time. Code receiving a Money parameter that trusts it to be immutable (e.g., checks a limit and stores it, uses it as a HashMap key, shares it across threads without synchronization) will be fooled: a malicious 'Money' returns 100 when checked and 1 billion when the transfer executes (a time-of-check/time-of-use bug). Therefore immutable classes should be final (or have a private constructor + static factory), and parameters from untrusted sources should be defensively copied into the standard immutable class.
key_points: A non-final class lets subclasses add mutable state and override accessors
Code trusting immutability is fooled (TOCTOU); make it final or use a private constructor, and copy defensively

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: Why is relying on finalize() to close files/connections a design mistake, and why has it been deprecated?
reference_answer: (1) There is no guarantee when finalize() will be called, or even whether it will be called before the program exits — OS resources (file handles, sockets) may run out before the GC runs. (2) Objects with finalize() slow down GC considerably (needing at least two cycles to reclaim). (3) finalize() can 'resurrect' the object by assigning this to a static variable, causing unpredictable behavior, and was exploited in 'finalizer attacks' to capture partially constructed objects. (4) Exceptions in finalize() are silently swallowed. Correct approach: implement AutoCloseable and use try-with-resources for deterministic release; Cleaner is only a last-resort safety net.
key_points: finalize() has no timing guarantee, slows GC, can resurrect objects and swallows exceptions
Use AutoCloseable + try-with-resources; Cleaner is only a safety net

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: An exception in finally loses the original exception
question: In legacy code using try { writeData(); } finally { connection.close(); }, if writeData() throws an IOException 'disk full' and then close() throws 'connection already closed', what happens to the error information? What about a return inside finally?
reference_answer: An exception thrown from finally completely REPLACES the exception being propagated: the caller only sees 'connection already closed' (a symptom) and entirely loses 'disk full' (the root cause), leading diagnosis in the wrong direction. Worse, if the finally block contains a return, every exception from try is silently swallowed and the method returns as if it succeeded. Fix: use try-with-resources (close exceptions become suppressed), or wrap close() in its own try-catch and call addSuppressed manually; never return/throw from finally.
key_points: An exception in finally overwrites and loses the original exception
return in finally swallows all exceptions; use try-with-resources or addSuppressed, never return/throw in finally

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: Why can't you directly call a method that throws IOException inside list.stream().map(f -> readFile(f)), and what are the trade-offs of the common workarounds?
reference_answer: The standard functional interfaces (Function, Consumer...) do not declare throws for checked exceptions, so a lambda cannot throw IOException outward. Workarounds: (1) catch and wrap into UncheckedIOException/RuntimeException — simple but loses the 'checked' nature, so callers are not reminded to handle it; (2) define a custom functional interface with throws plus an adapter utility — flexible but more code; (3) return a result type (Either/Result/Optional) per element to handle errors as data — explicit, does not abort the whole stream, but more complex; (4) use a plain for loop when error handling matters. The choice depends on whether an error should stop everything or just skip an element.
key_points: Standard functional interfaces do not allow throwing checked exceptions
Wrap as unchecked, custom interfaces, Result types or plain loops — each trades clarity against complexity

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: Default method conflicts when evolving an interface
question: A library adds a default method sort() to an interface MyList already implemented by thousands of classes. A client class already has a public void sort() method with different semantics (sorting descending). Analyze the consequences.
reference_answer: By the 'class wins' rule, the class's method takes precedence over the default method, so the client class still compiles — but their old method now unintentionally becomes the implementation of the interface's sort(). Library code calling myList.sort() expecting ascending order gets descending order: a silent semantic bug. If the signature differs in return type (int sort()), the class fails to compile after upgrading. Moreover, a shared default implementation may break the invariants of implementing classes (e.g., a default removeIf on a synchronized collection that does not hold the lock). Lesson: default methods are not 'free' — choose names unlikely to clash, document clearly, and treat adding methods to a public interface as a risky change.
key_points: Class wins: an existing class method silently becomes the implementation of the new default method
Can cause compile errors or broken invariants; adding default methods to a public interface is still risky

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: Static methods are hidden, not overridden
question: Class Parent has static void introduce() printing 'Parent', and class Child declares static void introduce() printing 'Child'. With Parent x = new Child(); x.introduce(); what is printed? Why is this a pitfall?
reference_answer: It prints 'Parent'. Static methods are bound at compile time based on the DECLARED TYPE of the variable, not the object's actual type; a static method with the same signature in a subclass only HIDES the superclass method rather than overriding it, so there is no polymorphism. Pitfall: calling through an object variable looks like a polymorphic call and developers expect 'Child'. Adding @Override to a static method causes a compile error, so @Override helps detect this; static methods should always be called via the class name.
key_points: Static methods bind at compile time by declared type; subclasses only hide them
Calling static methods via variables looks polymorphic; use @Override to detect and call via the class name

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: Overloading equals instead of overriding it
question: Class Point declares public boolean equals(Point other) { ... } (parameter of type Point instead of Object). Why does list.contains(new Point(1,2)) on an ArrayList<Point> still return false even though the list contains point (1,2)?
reference_answer: equals(Point) is an OVERLOAD, not an override of Object.equals(Object), because the signatures differ. Collections call o.equals(Object), so the method chosen is the default equals(Object) (reference comparison), never the custom one. Overloads are selected at compile time by the static type of the argument, while overrides are selected at runtime. The bug is silent because the code compiles fine, and calling p1.equals(p2) directly even gives the right result, causing confusion. Prevention: always declare equals(Object o) and annotate it with @Override so the compiler catches a wrong signature.
key_points: equals(Point) is an overload and does not override equals(Object), so collections never call it
Overloads are resolved at compile time by static type; use @Override with equals(Object)

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: Class Parent has private void validate() and public void process() which calls validate(). Class Child defines public void validate() with different logic. When calling new Child().process(), which validate() runs? What pitfall does this reveal?
reference_answer: Parent's validate() runs. Private methods are not inherited and therefore cannot be overridden; validate() in Child is an entirely new, unrelated method. The call to validate() inside Parent's process() is statically bound to Parent's private version. Pitfall: the subclass author thinks they are customizing the superclass behavior (as in Template Method) but it has no effect and no error is reported. To allow customization, the superclass must declare it protected (an intentional hook); always use @Override so the compiler reports an error when nothing is actually overridden.
key_points: Private methods are not inherited; a same-named method in the subclass is a new method
The superclass call still uses its private version; use protected hooks and @Override to allow customization

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: Anemic Domain Model vs Rich Domain Model
question: Analyze the trade-offs between an Anemic Domain Model (domain objects only have getters/setters, logic lives in Service classes) and a Rich Domain Model (domain objects contain both data and business behavior).
reference_answer: The Anemic Domain Model is simple, fits thin CRUD logic and maps easily to ORM/JSON, but it is essentially procedural programming dressed as objects: business invariants are not protected by the objects themselves (anyone can call setStatus), logic is duplicated across services, and invalid states are easy to create. The Rich Domain Model places behavior next to data (order.confirm(), order.addProduct()), protects invariants and expresses the business language, but requires more careful design, may conflict with frameworks requiring empty constructors/setters, and risks overloading entities with responsibilities or infrastructure dependencies. The choice should depend on the complexity of the business logic.
key_points: Anemic: simple, fits CRUD, but invariants are unprotected and logic is scattered
Rich: protects invariants and expresses the domain, but needs careful design and may conflict with frameworks

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: A team applies the Law of Demeter absolutely, adding to the Order class methods like getCustomerCity(), getCustomerBankName(), getCustomerCardExpiry()... Analyze the consequences and how to strike a balance.
reference_answer: Mechanical application turns Order into a 'Middle Man' with a bloated interface; every change in Customer requires another forwarding method in Order — coupling is not reduced, only hidden, and Order loses cohesion because it must know everything about customers. The Law of Demeter targets not depending on the internal structure of objects with behavior; it matters less for pure data structures (DTOs, value objects) and fluent/stream APIs. Balance: ask 'who should be responsible for this behavior' and move behavior to the right place (Tell, Don't Ask); if a client truly needs customer data, return an immutable value object/DTO instead of adding a series of delegating methods.
key_points: Absolute Demeter creates a Middle Man and a bloated interface; coupling is hidden, not reduced
Apply it to objects with behavior, not DTOs/fluent APIs; move behavior to the right place or return value objects

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: A Mediator turning into a God Object
question: A system uses a Mediator to coordinate 30 components of a ticket-booking screen. After a year, the mediator class is 4,000 lines long. Analyze the causes and how to address it.
reference_answer: A Mediator moves interaction complexity from the components into one place; if all coordination rules pile up there, it becomes a God Object: low cohesion, every change touches it, hard to test, frequent merge conflicts. Causes: not partitioning by interaction group, using the mediator for both business logic and UI logic. Remedies: split into several smaller mediators per group of tightly interacting components (flight selection, seat selection, payment), move business logic into domain services, shift some simple interactions to an event mechanism (observer) or an explicit state machine, and monitor size/cohesion metrics.
key_points: A Mediator that absorbs all coordination logic easily becomes a God Object
Split mediators by interaction group, move business logic to services, use events/state machines for simple parts

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: Analyze the common risks of using Chain of Responsibility in real systems (e.g., a loan approval processing chain).
reference_answer: (1) A request can travel through the whole chain without being handled — without a default handler at the end, it is silently 'swallowed'. (2) Handler order carries implicit business meaning: misconfiguring the order (checking limits before authentication) causes logic bugs or security holes. (3) A handler forgetting to call the next one breaks the chain. (4) Debugging and tracing are hard because control flow is distributed. (5) Long chains add latency and make performance guarantees harder. Mitigations: a default handler at the end that reports an explicit error, centralized order configuration with tests, logging/tracing at each step, and separating the 'who handles it' decision from forwarding.
key_points: Requests may go unhandled, handler order has implicit meaning, chains break easily
Need a default end handler, centralized tested ordering, and per-step logging/tracing

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: A developer saves memory by sharing TextStyle objects (font, size, color) among millions of characters, but TextStyle has a setColor() setter. Analyze the resulting bugs.
reference_answer: A flyweight is shared by many logical 'owners'; when one paragraph calls style.setColor(RED) to highlight a word, ALL other characters using that shared object also change color — a widespread semantic bug that is hard to trace. In a multi-threaded environment, modifying a shared object also causes race conditions. Moreover, the factory caches flyweights by key (font, size, color): modifying an object after caching makes the key and content diverge. Principle: flyweights must be immutable; a 'change' is done by obtaining another flyweight from the factory (factory.get(font, size, RED)), and the factory must be thread-safe (e.g., ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent).
key_points: Modifying a shared flyweight changes it everywhere it is referenced and causes race conditions
Flyweights must be immutable; obtain a different one from a thread-safe factory to 'change' it

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: Memory cost of Memento and alternatives
question: An image editor stores a Memento containing the whole image (50MB) after every operation to support 100 Undo steps. Analyze the problem and alternative designs.
reference_answer: Storing the entire state at every step costs up to 5GB of memory — infeasible. Options: (1) Command Pattern with undo: each operation stores enough information to reverse itself (a brighten command stores its parameters to darken back), small cost, but not every operation is exactly reversible (blur, cropping loses data). (2) Incremental mementos: store only the changed image tiles — deltas. (3) Hybrid: periodic full snapshots plus a sequence of commands/deltas in between; undo by restoring the nearest snapshot and replaying. (4) Share immutable structure (copy-on-write per tile) so mementos share unchanged parts. Also cap the number of steps or spill old history to disk.
key_points: Full snapshots at every step blow up memory
Alternatives: Command with undo, deltas/tiles, periodic snapshots + replay, copy-on-write structural sharing

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: The axis of change in Abstract Factory
question: A system uses Abstract Factory with a UIFactory interface providing createButton(), createDialog() and 5 implementations (Windows, Mac, Linux, Web, Mobile). Now a new product createSlider() is needed. Analyze the impact and the design lesson.
reference_answer: Abstract Factory is easy to extend along the 'add a new family' axis (add a factory implementing all methods), but very hard to extend along the 'add a new product type' axis: the method must be added to the interface and ALL 5 factories plus any external implementations must be changed (breaking compatibility if it is a public API). This illustrates that a pattern satisfies OCP along only one axis of change. Lesson: before choosing a pattern, identify which dimension changes more often; the impact can be reduced with a default method returning a generic implementation, a factory parameterized by product type (create(Class<T> type)) at the cost of type safety, or a registry of creators.
key_points: Abstract Factory makes adding families easy but adding product types hard (every factory must change)
Choose patterns by the main axis of change; mitigate with default methods, parameterized factories or registries

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: A team building a PDF report export feature set up Bridge, Abstract Factory and a plugin loader to 'support Excel, Word, HTML later', but two years later there is still only PDF. Analyze the cost of this decision.
reference_answer: This is the 'Speculative Generality' code smell (against YAGNI). Costs: (1) many classes and layers of indirection make code hard to read and hard for newcomers to follow; (2) abstractions based on guesses are often WRONG: when the Excel requirement actually arrives, it may need capabilities the interface did not anticipate (multiple sheets, formulas), forcing the whole structure to be reworked; (3) maintenance and testing cost for unused branches. A better approach: write simply for current needs while keeping code clean and tested; when a second or third variant appears, refactor to extract abstractions based on concrete cases ('rule of three').
key_points: Anticipatory abstraction adds complexity and maintenance cost without delivering value
Guess-based abstractions are often wrong; refactor when real variants appear (rule of three)

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: A global event bus and hidden coupling
question: An application uses a global EventBus: all modules publish/subscribe events via strings like 'order.updated'. Analyze the hidden problems of this architecture.
reference_answer: (1) Hidden coupling: modules still depend on each other through event names and payload structures, but these dependencies are invisible in the code (no imports/types); renaming an event or changing a payload breaks subscribers without the compiler noticing. (2) Control flow is hard to trace: who handles an event, and in what order? (3) Ordering and reentrancy: a subscriber publishing new events while handling one can cause infinite loops or inconsistent intermediate states. (4) Error handling: an exception in one subscriber may break others or be swallowed. (5) Memory leaks from forgetting to unsubscribe. Mitigations: use typed events (classes) instead of strings, scope buses per module, document event flows, and use direct calls when the relationship is a clear one-to-one.
key_points: An event bus creates hidden coupling through names/payloads that the compiler cannot check
Hard to trace, ordering/reentrancy risks, error propagation, leaks; use typed events and limited scopes

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: Circular dependencies in a DI container
question: In a Spring application, OrderService needs InventoryService via the constructor, and InventoryService needs OrderService. Analyze the resulting error and why 'fixing' it with field injection or @Lazy only hides the problem.
reference_answer: With constructor injection, the container cannot create either object first because each needs the other to exist — a startup error (BeanCurrentlyInCreationException). Switching to field/setter injection or @Lazy lets the container create the objects (assigning dependencies later or via a proxy), but the cycle remains: the two classes are tightly coupled in both directions, an object may be used before all dependencies are set, they are hard to test independently, and it usually signals a wrong split of responsibilities. Root-cause fixes: extract shared logic into a third class both depend on, invert one dependency via an interface/event (Order publishes an event, Inventory listens), or merge them if they are really one responsibility.
key_points: Constructor injection with a cycle prevents the container from instantiating the beans
Field injection/@Lazy only hide it; fix by extracting a shared class, inverting via interfaces/events, or merging

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: Overusing mocks couples tests to implementation
question: The test suite for a PaymentService mocks every dependency and verifies each internal call exactly (order, count, arguments). After a behavior-preserving refactoring, 40 tests fail. Analyze the cause and how to write more robust tests.
reference_answer: The tests verify HOW the class works (internal interaction details) rather than observable OUTCOMES — called over-specification. Any implementation change (merging two calls, reordering, adding caching) breaks tests even though behavior is correct, making tests an obstacle to refactoring and eroding trust ('red tests are normal'). Remedies: mock only at system boundaries with real side effects (payment gateway, email sending, time) and only verify interactions that are part of the business contract; use real objects or fakes for internal objects and value objects; prefer checking state/outputs; avoid mocking types you do not own and wrap them behind adapters instead.
key_points: Verifying internal interactions couples tests to implementation, breaking them on refactoring
Mock only at side-effect boundaries, prefer checking outcomes, use fakes/real objects internally

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: Value objects containing floating-point numbers and equality
question: A record Coordinate(double lat, double lon) is used as a HashMap key to group duplicate GPS points. Analyze the equals/hashCode issues with double.
reference_answer: (1) Floating-point error: two logically identical coordinates computed through different transformations (0.1 + 0.2 vs 0.3) have different bits and are not equal, splitting the key. (2) Records compare doubles with Double.compare, so 0.0 and -0.0 are considered DIFFERENT while NaN equals NaN — unlike the == operator, which is surprising. (3) Treating 'nearby' points as equal via an epsilon breaks the transitivity of equals and makes a consistent hashCode impossible. Approach: normalize to a discrete representation before using it as a key (round to a fixed number of digits, convert to integer micro-degrees, or a geohash), and use spatial structures (grids, KD-trees) for 'nearby' queries.
key_points: Floating-point error gives logically equal values different representations
Epsilon-based equals breaks transitivity; normalize to a discrete representation before using as a key

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: A system stores order status in the database using Status.ordinal() (0, 1, 2...). Analyze the risks as development continues.
reference_answer: ordinal() is the declaration position of the constant in the enum, depending on the order in the source code. Merely inserting a new status in the middle (e.g., PACKING between PAID and SHIPPING) or reordering makes every old database record be interpreted wrongly — silent data corruption with no error, very hard to detect and recover. The same applies to ordinals in serialized files, APIs or caches. Correct approach: store the constant's name (name()) or a stable code explicitly assigned in the enum (Status(int code) with a never-changing code field) with reverse mapping; with JPA use EnumType.STRING or an AttributeConverter.
key_points: ordinal depends on declaration order; inserting/reordering silently misinterprets old data
Store name() or an explicit stable code in the enum with reverse mapping

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: Shallow immutability of records and compact constructors
question: record Classroom(String code, List<Student> students) {} is advertised as immutable. Analyze why that is not entirely true and how to fix it with a compact constructor.
reference_answer: Records are only SHALLOWLY immutable: the students field is final and cannot be reassigned, but the List object inside is still mutable. A caller holding the original list passed to the constructor can modify it afterwards, and anyone calling classroom.students().add(...) can change the record's state — corrupting equals/hashCode if the record is a HashMap key. Fix with a compact constructor: record Classroom(String code, List<Student> students) { Classroom { Objects.requireNonNull(code); students = List.copyOf(students); } } — both validating and defensively copying into an immutable list. If Student elements are mutable, the record is still not deeply immutable.
key_points: Records are only shallowly immutable; mutable components can still be modified
Compact constructors validate and defensively copy (List.copyOf); mutable elements remain a risk

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: A system representing expression trees (Num, Add, Mul) needs to add both new NODE TYPES and new OPERATIONS (evaluate, print, simplify, differentiate). Compare the OOP polymorphism approach, Visitor, and sealed + pattern matching from the perspective of the 'Expression Problem'.
reference_answer: The Expression Problem states that it is hard to extend along both dimensions without modifying existing code while keeping type safety. OOP polymorphism (each node has evaluate(), print()): adding node types is easy (add a class), but adding operations requires modifying every class. Visitor and sealed + switch pattern matching: adding operations is easy (a new visitor/function), but adding node types requires modifying every visitor/switch — with sealed types, the compiler points out every place to update, safer than Visitor and with less boilerplate. The choice depends on which dimension changes more often: stable types with frequently added operations → sealed/Visitor; stable operations with frequently added types → OOP polymorphism. Advanced techniques (object algebras, type classes) solve both dimensions at the cost of complexity.
key_points: The Expression Problem: hard to extend both data types and operations simultaneously
OOP makes adding types easy, operations hard; Visitor/sealed the opposite; choose by main axis of change

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: Analyze the design and security risks when a business class implements Java's Serializable 'for convenience'.
reference_answer: (1) The serialized form becomes a hidden public API: every private field goes into the byte stream, and changing internal structure breaks compatibility with stored data (requiring serialVersionUID and version management). (2) Deserialization creates objects WITHOUT calling the constructor, so all invariant checks in the constructor are bypassed; an attacker can craft a byte stream producing an object in an invalid state (negative balance) or sharing references to internal mutable components. (3) 'Deserialization gadget chain' vulnerabilities allow remote code execution when deserializing untrusted data. Measures: avoid Java serialization for external data, use explicit formats (JSON with DTOs); if unavoidable, use the serialization proxy pattern, validate invariants and defensively copy in readObject, and use deserialization filters.
key_points: Serializable turns private structure into a hidden API that is hard to evolve
Deserialization bypasses constructors, breaks invariants and can be exploited for code execution; use DTOs/JSON or a serialization proxy

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: ThreadLocal memory leaks in thread pools
question: A UserContext class uses a static ThreadLocal<User> to store the current request's user in a web application running on a thread pool. Analyze two serious risks of not calling remove() after each request.
reference_answer: In a thread pool, threads are REUSED across many requests. (1) Data leaking between requests: if a later request does not overwrite the value (e.g., an anonymous request), it reads the previous request's User — a security hole (a user sees another user's data). (2) Memory leaks: values in ThreadLocalMap are strongly referenced and live as long as the thread (practically forever in a pool); if a value holds a large object graph or references the application's ClassLoader, the old ClassLoader cannot be reclaimed on redeploy (PermGen/Metaspace leak). Measures: always set/remove in try-finally (or in a filter/interceptor), avoid storing large objects, consider passing context explicitly or using ScopedValue.
key_points: Threads are reused, so an old ThreadLocal value can leak into another request
Values live with the thread causing memory/ClassLoader leaks; always remove in finally

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: equals/hashCode of ORM entities with generated IDs
question: A JPA entity Order overrides equals/hashCode based on the id field generated by the database on persist. A new object (id = null) is added to a HashSet and then saved to the database. Analyze the bug.
reference_answer: Before persisting, id = null so hashCode is computed from null (or all new entities are 'equal' if equals compares null ids). After persisting, id gets a value so hashCode changes — the entity is now in the wrong bucket of the HashSet: contains() returns false, remove() fails, duplicates can be added. Also, several new entities with null ids may be treated as duplicates and dropped from the Set. Solutions: use an immutable natural business key (order number) for equals/hashCode; or generate the id on the application side (UUID) right at construction; or equals by id but hashCode returning a per-class constant (accepting lower performance) and treating id-null objects as equal only to themselves. Also be careful with getClass/instanceof because ORMs create proxy subclasses.
key_points: The id assigned on persist changes hashCode, losing the entity in a HashSet; null-id entities may be treated as duplicates
Use an immutable business key, early-generated ids (UUID), or a constant hashCode; mind ORM proxies

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: The getter public Config getConfig() { if (config == null) config = readFromFile(); return config; } is called concurrently from many threads. Analyze the bugs that can occur besides reading the file multiple times.
reference_answer: (1) Race condition: several threads see null and all call readFromFile(), wasting resources; if Config has side effects (opening connections, registrations), multiple instances coexist and threads hold different objects, causing inconsistent state. (2) Memory visibility: without synchronization, a thread may see a non-null config reference while the fields inside Config are not fully written (a half-built object) due to reordering. (3) A thread might never see the assigned value. Solutions: eager initialization if the cost is acceptable; the holder idiom; synchronized/volatile with correct double-checked locking; or AtomicReference/ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent; Config should be immutable with final fields.
key_points: Race conditions create multiple instances, with threads holding different objects
Without synchronization a half-built object may be seen; use the holder idiom, volatile, computeIfAbsent, immutable objects

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: A custom Iterator that breaks the contract
question: A class implements a custom Iterator over data read from a file, where hasNext() reads ahead one line and advances the file pointer. Analyze the subtle bugs relative to the Iterator contract.
reference_answer: The implicit contract: hasNext() must be idempotent with no observable side effects — calling it several times in a row must not change the element next() will return. If each hasNext() reads another line, calling hasNext() twice (common in debugging code or libraries) skips data. Other bugs: next() when exhausted must throw NoSuchElementException rather than return null; an unsupported remove() must throw UnsupportedOperationException; the iterator holds a file resource with no way to close it if the client stops midway. Correct approach: use a 'read-ahead' buffer variable (lookahead) — hasNext() only reads when the buffer is empty, next() takes from the buffer and clears it — and consider combining with AutoCloseable or a Stream with onClose.
key_points: hasNext() must be idempotent and not consume data; next() must throw NoSuchElementException when exhausted
Use a lookahead buffer, handle remove() and resource release correctly

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: Analyze common misuses of Optional: as an entity field type, as a method parameter, calling get() without checking, and Optional<List<T>>.
reference_answer: (1) Optional as a field: Optional is not Serializable, adds an extra object per field, and was not designed for this — an absent field should be null internally with a getter returning Optional. (2) Optional as a parameter: forces callers to wrap values, and null can still be passed for the Optional itself (now three states); use overloads or a documented nullable parameter. (3) opt.get() without checking just turns a NullPointerException into a NoSuchElementException, defeating the purpose; use orElse/orElseThrow with a clear message, map/flatMap. (4) Optional<List<T>>: collections already have a natural 'empty' state, so return an empty list instead of an Optional. Also, orElse(expensiveComputation()) always evaluates its argument; use orElseGet(() -> ...) for lazy evaluation.
key_points: Optional is meant for return types; not for fields, parameters, or wrapping collections
Unchecked get() is pointless; use orElseThrow/map, and orElseGet for expensive defaults

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: Class Notification has a Builder; subclass EmailNotification needs a Builder that adds a subject() method. Why might new EmailNotification.Builder().content("x").subject("y") fail to compile, and what technique fixes it? What are the trade-offs?
reference_answer: content() declared in the parent Builder returns the parent Builder type, so after calling it the static type of the expression is the parent Builder — which lacks subject(), causing a compile error even though the actual object is the child Builder. Fix with the 'generic self-type' (curiously recurring template) pattern: abstract static class Builder<T extends Builder<T>> { T content(String s) { ...; return self(); } protected abstract T self(); }, with the child Builder declared as extends Notification.Builder<Builder> and implementing self() to return this. Trade-offs: complex generic signatures, hard for newcomers to read, lots of boilerplate, and it still cannot prevent a subclass from declaring the wrong type argument; with multiple inheritance levels complexity grows quickly — consider composition or a record + separate builder.
key_points: Parent builder methods return the parent type, losing child builder methods in the call chain
Use a generic self-type (T extends Builder<T>, self()); trade-offs are complexity and boilerplate

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: To save memory, a system canonicalizes (interns) ProductCode objects using a static HashMap<String, ProductCode> cache: each code has exactly one object. After a few weeks, the application runs out of memory. Analyze and propose a solution.
reference_answer: A static HashMap holds STRONG references to every key and value ever canonicalized and never removes them — including product codes that appeared once and are never used again. The cache grows without bound with the number of distinct codes seen, causing a memory leak despite the original goal of saving memory. Solutions: use weak references so objects no longer used can be reclaimed by the GC (a WeakHashMap with values wrapped in WeakReference, because if the value strongly references the key the entry is never removed), or use a bounded cache by size/time (LRU, Caffeine), or intern only finite, known value sets. The cache must also be thread-safe.
key_points: A static canonical cache holds strong references forever and grows unboundedly
Use WeakHashMap + WeakReference values, or a size/time-bounded thread-safe cache

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: The cost of polymorphic calls in high-performance code
question: In a loop processing 100 million elements, calling shape.area() through an interface with 8 implementing classes is significantly slower than when there is only 1 implementing class. Explain the cause at the JVM level and the trade-offs of optimizing.
reference_answer: The JVM's JIT optimizes virtual calls by profiling the actual types at each call site: if it sees only 1 type (monomorphic) or 2 types (bimorphic), it can inline the method body directly, enabling further optimizations (removing checks, vectorization). When a call site sees many types (megamorphic), the JIT must use virtual method table lookups (vtable/itable) and cannot inline, which is much slower in tight loops. Possible optimizations: group data by type and process each group (each loop monomorphic), use columnar data structures instead of polymorphic objects, or switch over a sealed type. Trade-off: sacrificing extensibility and clarity of the OOP design; only do this after measurements prove it is a real hotspot.
key_points: The JIT inlines monomorphic/bimorphic calls, while megamorphic ones need table lookups and cannot be inlined
Optimize by grouping by type, columnar data, or sealed switches; trades extensibility, only after profiling

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: Treating remote calls like local calls
question: A system uses a Remote Proxy so clients call customer.getName(), customer.getEmail(), customer.getAddress()... as if on a local object, but each getter is actually a network request. Analyze the problems and the principles for designing interfaces of distributed objects.
reference_answer: The proxy makes remote calls look local, hiding fundamental differences (the 'fallacies of distributed computing'): (1) latency — a 'chatty' interface with many small getters turns one screen into dozens of round trips, hundreds of times slower; (2) partial failure — each getter may fail due to network errors or timeouts, but the method signature does not express that; (3) consistency — reading fields one by one at different times may mix data from two versions. Principles: design remote interfaces to be 'coarse-grained' — one call returns a complete DTO (Remote Facade + Data Transfer Object), make network errors and timeouts explicit in the API, and design idempotent operations so they can be retried safely.
key_points: Remote calls differ fundamentally from local ones: latency, partial failure, consistency
Design coarse-grained interfaces (Remote Facade + DTO), make network errors explicit, keep operations idempotent for retries

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
concept: Calling alien methods while holding a lock in Observer
question: A Warehouse class (subject) implements updateStock() as synchronized, and inside it loops over the observer list calling observer.changed(this). Analyze the deadlock risk and other concurrency bugs.
reference_answer: Calling observers while holding a lock means calling 'alien methods': Warehouse does not control what observers do. If an observer, in changed(), waits for another lock held by a second thread, while that second thread needs to call a synchronized method of Warehouse → deadlock. Slow observers (sending email, network calls) hold the lock for a long time, blocking all other threads. An observer calling back into Warehouse and unsubscribing itself during iteration causes ConcurrentModificationException (or reentrancy changing state midway). Fix: inside the synchronized block only update state and take a snapshot of the observer list (or use CopyOnWriteArrayList), then NOTIFY OUTSIDE the synchronized block ('open call'); consider asynchronous notification via an executor.
key_points: Calling observer callbacks while holding a lock can cause deadlocks, blocking and reentrancy bugs
Update state inside the lock, snapshot the observers, then notify outside the lock (open call) or asynchronously

subject: Object-Oriented Programming
question: To avoid null, a Cart class uses private static final List<Product> EMPTY = new ArrayList<>(); and the default constructor sets this.items = EMPTY. Analyze the bug that appears when the system runs in production.
reference_answer: Every Cart created with the default constructor shares the SAME ArrayList EMPTY. When one cart calls items.add(p), the product is added to the shared list, so every other 'empty' cart (of other users) suddenly contains it too — data leaking between users, and in a multi-threaded environment the ArrayList structure can also be corrupted. 'final' only prevents reassigning EMPTY; it does not make the list immutable. Correct approach: create a new list for each object (this.items = new ArrayList<>()), or if a shared default is desired it must be truly immutable (List.of()) and code adding elements must replace it with a new list (copy-on-write). This is also the classic 'mutable default argument' pitfall in Python.
key_points: A shared mutable default object makes changes in one object leak into all others
final does not make the list immutable; create one per instance or share only truly immutable values
